17: The surprises trace back to Spring's proxy model. @Transactional applies only when a call crosses the proxy, so self-invocation can bypass the annotated boundary. Visibility, proxy type, and configuration also affect interception. Rollback defaults are another trap: unchecked exceptions and errors roll back, while checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor says otherwise. A database transaction does not make remote calls atomic, and wrapping slow network work holds locks and connections longer than intended. Work moved to @Async or another thread does not inherit the transaction context. Put the boundary on an injected component, keep remote work outside it, and verify commit, rollback, propagation, and lock behavior with integration tests against a real database.
19: Design retries by assigning one owner for each failure path; otherwise controller, service, and client retries multiply load during the outage. Retry only plausibly transient failures, never validation or domain rejection. Require an idempotency guarantee before retrying writes, and keep every attempt inside one caller deadline with bounded attempts, exponential backoff, jitter, and Retry-After support. Coordinate retries with circuit breaking, admission control, and queues so recovery traffic does not overwhelm the dependency again. Make retryability part of the client contract rather than hidden configuration. Measure attempts, final outcomes, added latency, deadline exhaustion, and amplification by dependency. A useful test forces timeouts and partial success, then proves exactly one layer retries and the total work remains bounded.
22: Resilience settings must come from an explicit failure policy, not copied defaults. Split the user-facing deadline across hops before choosing timeouts; a 500 ms SLO cannot contain three 400 ms dependency budgets. Size concurrency and queues from measured downstream capacity, with defined rejection behavior. Configure a breaker from observed failure distributions and enough samples to avoid opening on normal tail noise. Define which failures retry, when to fail fast, and whether a fallback is genuinely independent and acceptable to the product. Then prove the configuration with latency, error, and saturation tests. Expose attempts, rejections, timeouts, open circuits, and fallback outcomes per dependency. Give every configuration an owner and review date, because traffic and dependency behavior change while copied settings silently rot.
26: Idempotency is a storage and recovery contract, not just a request header. Scope a client-generated key to the authenticated caller and operation, then atomically persist the key, normalized request fingerprint, status, and result under a unique constraint. The first request reserves the key; a concurrent duplicate receives a defined in-progress response, and a completed duplicate receives the stored result without re-execution. Reject reuse of the key with a different payload. Design the crash window between the external side effect and result persistence: propagate the key downstream, query the downstream outcome, or reconcile safely before retrying. Retain records for at least the documented client retry horizon. Test concurrent duplicates and lost responses, and monitor duplicate hits, fingerprint mismatches, in-progress collisions, and reconciliation failures.
32: Start with workload-specific latency, residency, cost, RTO, and RPO; multi-region is not one topology. Reads can often use regional replicas with explicit staleness. Writes may use a home region with asynchronous replication, synchronous replication when data loss is unacceptable, or active-active only when the product defines conflict semantics. Design traffic steering, control-plane failure, fencing of the old writer, in-flight work, and failback reconciliation. Remove hidden dependencies on one region and provision enough spare capacity to absorb failover traffic. Do not claim instant recovery or zero RPO without mechanisms that prove it. Rehearse failover and failback under load, inject partitions, and measure actual recovery time, data loss, split-brain prevention, and regional saturation against the stated objectives.
38: Choose a partition key from the dominant latency-sensitive access patterns: the key should keep common queries local rather than forcing fan-out. Then test distribution across data size, write rate, and computation using production-shaped tenant and traffic histograms, not averages. Avoid monotonic keys that concentrate current writes and celebrity keys where one tenant dominates a shard. Account for cross-partition transactions, secondary-index fan-out, rebalancing, and future key evolution. If tenant ID preserves locality but one tenant owns 20 percent of traffic, consider salting a write hotspot, splitting that tenant, or isolating it rather than accepting a permanently hot partition. Validate with traffic replay and monitor the hottest partition, queueing, storage growth, and rebalance cost. A key is good only if both access locality and tail distribution remain acceptable as the workload grows.
43: Derive tenant context from authenticated identity at the trusted edge; never trust a caller-provided tenant identifier by itself. Propagate that context explicitly and enforce it at multiple layers according to risk: API authorization, tenant-scoped service and repository APIs, database policies or schema boundaries, queue metadata, storage prefixes, and IAM conditions. Each layer should limit the blast radius of a defect above it. Give privileged and break-glass flows separate, time-bound authorization with complete audit records. Decide when a large or regulated tenant needs stronger physical isolation rather than row scoping alone. Keep the design honest with continuous negative tests that attempt cross-tenant access through every identifier and asynchronous path. Monitor denied access, privileged actions, missing tenant context, and policy exceptions so isolation remains verifiable after years of change.
48: Treat guardrails as a platform product: a control that teams bypass protects nothing. Centralize high-value repeatable controls in base images, templates, libraries, and CI so the secure path is easier than the insecure path. Keep every policy transparent, versioned, testable, and tied to a named threat. Fail clearly at the boundary and explain remediation rather than silently rewriting deployments and teaching teams the wrong system model. Provide a visible exception path with an owner, expiry, compensating controls, and review; that safety valve prevents hidden bypasses while preserving delivery for unusual cases. Measure adoption, false positives, bypasses, exception age, and incident outcomes. If bypasses rise, improve the guardrail and migration support instead of treating friction as a discipline problem.
51: Requests drive scheduling and reserved capacity; limits are kernel-enforced ceilings. CPU above a limit is throttled, while memory above a limit usually ends in an OOM kill. Requests and limits also affect QoS and eviction priority under node pressure, so they are availability controls, not form fields. Derive them from steady-state, burst, rollout, and failure measurements. HPA utilization is calculated against requests, so a bad request distorts scaling. For Java, budget the whole process, not only heap: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache, and GC overhead can trigger a container OOM while heap looks healthy. CPU quota can also stretch latency-sensitive JVM work despite modest average CPU. Verify choices with throttling, RSS, heap and native memory, restarts, probe behavior, p99 latency, and autoscaling under representative load.
54: Split Terraform state by environment, ownership, lifecycle, and blast radius. Avoid one global lock and avoid thousands of arbitrary tiny states; a practical production split often separates network, data, platform, and application resources so routine app changes cannot endanger a database. Resources whose replacement destroys data deserve isolated state, restricted permissions, and slower review gates. Store state remotely with encryption, locking, backups, versioning, access control, and audit; treat read access as sensitive because providers may persist secrets. Promote code and pinned provider versions between environments, never copy state. Expose deliberate outputs instead of coupling consumers to implementation details. Rehearse import, moved-block, restore, and replacement workflows, and add policy that blocks destructive changes to protected resource classes before apply.
61: In the first 15 minutes, establish customer impact, scope, severity, and one incident commander. Create a single source of truth, then assign operations, investigation, communication, and scribe roles so work is coordinated instead of duplicated. Stabilization outranks diagnosis: freeze concurrent changes and choose reversible containment such as stopping a rollout, shedding traffic, or isolating a dependency. Keep the timeline explicit and separate confirmed facts from hypotheses. Set a communication cadence early and update stakeholders even when the status is unchanged. Escalate domain expertise before the team spends an hour guessing, and control who may make changes while evidence is being gathered. Success at minute 15 is bounded impact, clear authority, preserved evidence, named workstreams, and a known next update, not a prematurely declared root cause.
64: Design degradation before an incident by ranking capabilities with product partners. Preserve core invariants and high-priority paths, then shed optional enrichment, stale-tolerant reads, or expensive computation in a deliberate order. Some expensive work, such as audit or security controls, may remain non-sheddable. Encode the ladder as configuration so response is execution rather than debate. Make degraded state visible to users and operators, including which rung is active and why. Verify that each fallback is independent and capacity-tested; redirecting every service to the same cache can turn the fallback into the next outage. Test entry, sustained operation, and recovery under overload and dependency failure. Measure shed work, fallback errors, core-path SLOs, dependency saturation, and time to return to normal without leaving permanent degraded behavior behind.
68: Influence without authority means designing conditions other teams choose to adopt. Start with their goals, constraints, incentives, and decision rights; a proposal that ignores how they are measured is easy to reject. Build credibility by listening and producing evidence that answers their objections, such as a focused prototype or pilot. Co-design the path and lower adoption cost with tooling, migration help, defaults, and clear ownership rather than issuing a compliance demand. Use escalation only for genuine safety boundaries or unresolved decision deadlock, because unnecessary escalation spends trust. Measure adoption and outcomes after your direct attention moves elsewhere. If usage collapses when office hours stop, you created dependence rather than influence. Durable influence leaves the paved road, exception ownership, and decision process embedded with the adopting teams.
74: Freeze deployments and migrations first so the combined state stops changing. Establish customer impact, then determine exactly which schema changes committed, what partial data exists, which application versions are running, and whether transactions or background work remain in flight. Choose rollback, roll-forward, or traffic isolation from reversibility and version compatibility, not preference. If the old application cannot read the committed schema, rollback is unavailable; isolate damaging writes and roll forward a tolerant reader. Preserve a forensic snapshot before repair, validate data invariants, and reconcile partial work idempotently. Recovery is complete only when compatible versions are serving, data is consistent, and queued work is safe. Prevent recurrence with expand-contract migrations, explicit schema/application sequencing, compatibility gates, and rehearsed recovery tests.
75: Do not apply. A database replacement is a data-migration event, not a routine infrastructure change. Compare three artifacts until every destructive line is explained: live infrastructure, Terraform state, and intended configuration. Common causes include a provider schema change, a renamed resource address, drift, or a missing import. Protect the resource and capture current state plus tested data backups before any repair. Rehearse provider migration, moved blocks, state moves, or imports against a non-production copy of state, then require peer review. If replacement is genuinely required, design replication, cutover, validation, rollback, and RPO/RTO explicitly. Prevent recurrence by pinning providers, reviewing plans on dependency bumps, isolating database state, and enforcing policy that blocks replacement of protected resource classes unless an approved migration workflow is active.
77: Reframe the dispute as risk management, not security versus delivery. Clarify the protected asset, threat, likelihood, impact, and any non-negotiable compliance obligation behind the proposed control. Decompose the two-month plan and look for a safer delivery shape: reduce scope, sequence the sensitive capability later, gate it behind a feature flag, or use a temporary compensating control such as manual approval. Make residual risk explicit and have the accountable authority accept it in writing. Every exception needs an owner, expiry, verification, and a dated plan for the full control; never allow an informal waiver that silently becomes permanent. Track both delivery and risk outcomes, then verify that the compensating control expires and the promised control ships. A narrower honest launch is better than either unmanaged exposure or an unexplained blanket delay.
99: Treat a new sealed subtype as both a source-compatibility and distributed-contract change. Inventory exhaustive switches, serializers, persisted data, and independently deployed consumers. Code you control may benefit from compile failures, but an old service receiving a new discriminator needs a safe unknown-variant path rather than a crash. Roll out tolerant readers before any producer emits the subtype, publish consumer contract tests and compatibility guidance, and monitor deployed consumer versions plus unknown-result telemetry. Only enable writers after incompatible readers are gone. If ordering must compress, use a temporary translation to an older meaning and measure its semantic loss. For public hierarchies that evolve independently, consider a permanent Unknown representation. Bound the compatibility window and remove shims only after adoption evidence proves they are no longer used.
111: Start by separating profile fields by conflict semantics. Preferences may tolerate deterministic last-write handling, edits to different fields can merge, unique usernames require one authority or coordination, and regulated identity fields may need a home region. Choose among home-region routing, per-field merge with version metadata, explicit conflict presentation, or consensus only where the invariant justifies its latency and availability cost. Never apply one last-write-wins rule to the whole profile without product approval, because it silently loses concurrent edits. Make replication idempotent and run anti-entropy repair so divergence heals. Design failover and failback with residency constraints, auditability, and conflict visibility. Test partitions, clock skew, simultaneous edits, duplicate replication, and regional recovery, then monitor merge conflicts and repair lag.
